questions.stem: What makes all the atoms of one element identical to each other?

options.text: They all contain the same number of protons
options.explanation: One proton count across every atom is the defining feature of an element.

options.text: They all have the same mass
options.explanation: Neutron numbers can differ between atoms of the same element, so mass is not the marker.

options.text: They all look the same under a microscope
options.explanation: Appearance is not the chemical criterion; atoms of one element share a proton count, not looks.

options.text: They all refuse to bond with anything
options.explanation: Elements do react and bond; the definition concerns proton count, not reactivity.

questions.stem: A student claims that because copper cannot be split into anything simpler, copper can never change at all. What is the flaw?

options.text: Cannot be split refers to separating it into simpler substances, not to chemical change
options.explanation: Copper stays an element only while unbonded; it readily takes part in reactions that build compounds.

options.text: Copper is actually a compound, so the claim fails twice
options.explanation: Copper holds one proton count throughout, which is exactly what an element is.

options.text: Splitting and reacting are the same process described in two words
options.explanation: Splitting means separating into simpler parts; reacting means bonding to build new substances.

options.text: Copper can be split if heated gently enough
options.explanation: No physical method, gentle or harsh, divides an element into simpler substances.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide contains carbon and oxygen. Why is it a compound rather than a mixture?

options.text: The two elements are chemically combined into one fixed substance
options.explanation: Chemical bonds join the carbon to the oxygen, which is precisely the compound criterion.

options.text: It contains two different substances floating loosely together
options.explanation: The carbon and oxygen are bonded into one substance, not floating separately.

options.text: It is made of molecules, and every molecule is a compound
options.explanation: An oxygen molecule pairs two identical atoms and stays an element, so molecule does not imply compound.

options.text: Because it is a gas at room temperature
options.explanation: State of matter has no bearing on class; gases can be elements, compounds or mixtures.

questions.stem: Which line classifies copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4, correctly?

options.text: A compound, because three elements are chemically combined within it
options.explanation: Copper, sulfur and oxygen are bonded into one substance, which is the compound definition at work.

options.text: An element, because the name begins with copper
options.explanation: The name borrows from copper, but the substance holds three elements bonded together.

options.text: A mixture, because it contains several substances
options.explanation: It is one bonded substance, not several substances placed side by side.

options.text: None of the three, because salts sit outside the classes
options.explanation: The three classes cover every substance; a pure salt sits inside the compound class.

questions.stem: A poster sorts substances into four boxes: element, compound, mixture and other. What is wrong with the fourth box?

options.text: It is unnecessary, because the first three already cover every substance
options.explanation: The three-way sort is exhaustive, so the fourth box stays empty forever.

options.text: Some substances are part element and part compound by nature
options.explanation: A substance is one or the other; hybrid classes do not exist in this scheme.

options.text: The boxes apply only to pure samples prepared in a laboratory
options.explanation: Every substance anywhere — sand, air, milk — falls into one of the three classes.

options.text: The fourth box is needed for elements not yet discovered
options.explanation: Any future substance will still be an element, a compound or a mixture.

questions.stem: Stirring sand into water gives cloudy water. How is the result classified, and why?

options.text: A mixture — the sand and the water are not chemically combined
options.explanation: Two substances sharing a space with no bonds between them form a mixture.

options.text: A compound — two substances have combined into one
options.explanation: Combining without chemical bonds is mixing, not compound formation.

options.text: An element — only one kind of liquid is visible
options.explanation: Visibility decides nothing about class; two substances are present even if one is hidden from view.

options.text: A compound, because the sand dissolves into the water
options.explanation: The sand does not dissolve here; and even dissolving leaves a mixture, never a compound.

questions.stem: Why can filtration or evaporation separate the ingredients of a mixture but never the elements inside a compound?

options.text: Mixtures hold no chemical bonds to break, so physical methods suffice
options.explanation: Physical methods cannot break chemical bonds, which is why compounds resist every one of them.

options.text: Physical methods are simply too weak to disturb a compound
options.explanation: Strength is not the issue; no physical process targets the bonds inside a compound.

options.text: Compounds separate when heated to a high enough temperature
options.explanation: Decomposition by heat is a chemical change, not a physical separation.

options.text: Filtration works on compounds provided the filter paper is fine enough
options.explanation: Filter fineness cannot undo chemical combination.

questions.stem: A particle diagram shows three separate two-atom units, each bonding one black sphere to one white sphere, and nothing else. What is shown?

options.text: A compound — one kind of chemically combined atom pair, repeated
options.explanation: Identical bonded pairs of two different atoms depict a single compound.

options.text: A mixture of two elements
options.explanation: The spheres are bonded in pairs, not loose, and each pair holds two different atoms.

options.text: An element, because every unit looks the same
options.explanation: Sameness of unit with two different atom types is the compound signature.

options.text: A mixture of two compounds
options.explanation: Only one kind of unit is present, so nothing is mixed.

questions.stem: Oil floated on water is shaken and then settles back into two layers. Classify the result and justify it.

options.text: A mixture — two substances in contact with no chemical combination
options.explanation: Layering changes nothing; the oil and the water remain separate substances.

options.text: A compound — the shaking made them combine
options.explanation: Shaking mixes; it does not bond, and the layers returning is itself evidence of no bonding.

options.text: A compound, because the boundary between the layers is sharp
options.explanation: A sharp boundary shows the substances refused to combine — the mark of a mixture.

options.text: An element, because water is present
options.explanation: Water is itself a compound, and its presence alongside oil makes the whole a mixture.

questions.stem: The exam hands you an unfamiliar substance described only in words and asks which of the three classes it belongs to. What habit earns the marks?

options.text: Ask two questions: are all atoms the same kind, and are different atoms chemically joined
options.explanation: Same atoms means element; different atoms bonded means compound; different substances unbonded means mixture.

options.text: Name its state of matter first, since class depends on it
options.explanation: Solid, liquid or gas, the three classes apply equally; state is irrelevant.

options.text: Guess element whenever the sample has a single colour
options.explanation: Colour carries no class information at all.

options.text: Call any white powder a mixture to be safe
options.explanation: Classification is decided by structure, not hedging; many white powders are pure compounds.
